structure.title: Growing with Purpose, Touching Lives Globally
structure.summary: Sun Pharma's purpose-driven journey to enhance global healthcare by improving medicine accessibility and patient outcomes. FY25 progress across growth pillars: Specialty, India, and Emerging Markets. Highlights include US FDA approval of Leqselvi for severe alopecia areata, strategic alliances like Philogen for anti-cancer immunotherapy, and acquisition of Checkpoint Therapeutics for an immuno-oncology asset. Maintained growth momentum in India and global markets through broad portfolio and field strength. Embedded sustainability via energy usage, emission reduction, water stewardship, waste management, ethical governance, and community well-being, recognized in S&P Global Sustainability Yearbook 2025. Future focus: breakthrough innovation, scaling in key therapeutic areas, differentiated assets, and agility amid dynamic regulatory landscapes in over 100 countries. Also notes 40 global manufacturing sites across six continents and 43,000+ global employees.

structure.title: Sun Pharma at a Glance Driving Impact through Access and Innovation
key_items: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs); Generic and Branded Generic Medicines
structure.summary: Sun Pharma is a global specialty generics company with a diversified portfolio of innovative medicines, generics, consumer healthcare, and APIs, operating in over 100 countries. It invests 6-8% of revenue in R&D across six global centers with 2,900+ researchers. The specialty business focuses on dermatology, ophthalmology, and onco-dermatology with 26 innovative products. Consumer healthcare covers OTC products in 25+ countries, and the API portfolio includes 400+ products. Revenue is diversified across India (33%), US (31%), emerging markets (18%), RoW (14%), and API/others (4%). It is India's largest pharmaceutical company and the 12th largest generic company in the US, offering various dosage forms.

nodes.summary: Chairman Dilip Shanghvi's message reviews Sun Pharma's FY24-25 robust growth, strategic progress, and adaptability amid industry changes like COVID-19, generic price erosion, and geopolitical uncertainties. Challenges include on-shoring demand, price pressures, and diverse regulations, mitigated by diversification and risk management. Financials show revenue up 9% to ₹520B, EBITDA up 17.3% to ₹153B, and net profit up 19% to ₹120B. Global Specialty revenue share rose to 20%, with increased R&D spend to US$154M. structure.title: Management Discussion and Analysis
structure.summary: The text covers the global pharmaceutical industry's transformative phase, including spending trends projected to exceed $2.3 trillion by 2028 with a 5-8% CAGR, volume growth of 2.3% driven by emerging markets like China, India, Southeast Asia, and Latin America, while mature markets moderate. structure.title: Key Trends and Growth Drivers Shaping the Future
structure.summary: The text covers key trends and growth drivers in the pharmaceutical/healthcare sector. It discusses per capita consumption disparities, noting higher usage in Japan and Western Europe versus developing regions, with access challenges in Africa and the Middle East. Global demographic dynamics are highlighted, including ageing populations, evolving disease burdens, and younger populations with rising incomes. It addresses the rise of innovative therapies such as biologics, small molecules, and precision treatments, and the shifting therapeutic landscape toward oncology, immunology, and endocrinology. Key trends include supply chain and operational agility through real-time analytics and AI-led forecasting, and digital health and advanced analytics transforming drug discovery, clinical trials, and patient engagement.

structure.title: Budget Pressures and Cost Containment
structure.summary: The section on budget pressures and cost containment covers pharmaceutical spending trends and strategies across developed markets, the US, Western Europe (WE5), Japan, pharmerging markets, and India. It highlights cost containment through generics, biosimilars, value-based reimbursement, and pricing policies. Developed markets face budget pressures with spending projected to reach $1.775-1.805 trillion by 2028, driven by innovative therapeutics despite generic/biosimilar competition. The US sees invoice spending growth of $299 billion, offset by loss of exclusivity and slower biosimilar uptake, with net spending rising more modestly. WE5 growth is driven by new brand launches, while Japan's spending remains flat due to price revisions. Pharmerging markets grow through generics and non-originator medicines, constrained by budgets. India is projected to reach $38-42 billion by 2028, driven by access expansion, generics, and rising chronic diseases.

nodes.title: US 1
nodes.summary: The text projects US pharmaceutical spending growth through 2028, with invoice-level spending increasing by approximately US$299 billion, driven by protected branded products (US$322 billion) and over 250 new active substances (US$119 billion), particularly in oncology, immunology, diabetes, and obesity. Headwinds include loss of exclusivity reducing brand spending by US$145 billion and slower-than-expected biosimilar uptake. Net spending is projected to rise more modestly by US$91 billion, reaching US$1,010 billion at invoice prices by 2028, with the gap between invoice and net spending widening due to discounts and rebates, expanding from 37% in 2023 to 47% by 2028 under the Inflation Reduction Act. Overall, the market grows on innovation but faces intensifying pricing pressures and competition. A graph shows US pharmaceutical spending and growth, with 2019-2023 CAGR of 7.6% and 2024-2028 CAGR of 6-9%.

Over 175 new active substances are expected, led by oncology, neurology, and rare diseases. Japan's spending remains nearly flat due to annual price revisions and a shift toward protected brands and generics. Pharmerging markets expand through generic and non-originator medicines, with limited specialty uptake due to budget constraints. Key themes include pricing policies, biosimilar adoption, and access to innovation.

nodes.title: Japan 1
nodes.summary: The text covers pharmaceutical market trends: generics/biosimilars contributing $18B growth over five years despite price erosion; over 175 new active substances launching by 2028, with oncology dominant, plus neurology, rare diseases, and next-gen biotherapeutics like cell/gene therapies; high costs prompting value assessments. It details Japan's flat spending (-2% to 1% growth) due to pricing policies, rising protected brand share (48% to 54%), declining long-listed products (24% to 11% to 7% by 2028), and increased generics adoption. Pharmerging markets show volume-driven growth from generics and non-originator brands, with specialty medicines at 13% share, constrained budgets, low prices, and infrastructure/reimbursement limitations, though healthcare coverage and local manufacturing support growth.

structure.title: Government grants
structure.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for government grants and employee benefits. It categorizes financial assets and liabilities by measurement basis: fair value through profit or loss, fair value through other comprehensive income, and amortised cost, listing items such as investments, loans, trade receivables, cash, borrowings, payables, and lease liabilities with corresponding amounts in millions as at March 31, 2024. A footnote excludes investments in subsidiaries and associates measured at cost. The fair value hierarchy table discloses Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 classifications for financial assets (quoted and unquoted equity investments, derivatives) and financial liabilities (derivatives) measured at fair value on a recurring basis as at March 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Financial liabilities

nodes.title: Hedges of highly probable forecasted transactions
nodes.summary: The text covers hedge accounting for highly probable forecasted transactions, detailing cash flow hedges, effective and ineffective portions, and recorded gains/losses for 2025 and 2024. It also discusses foreign exchange derivative contracts not designated as hedges, interest rate risk (no exposure due to fixed rates), and commodity rate risk (no material derivatives). Additionally, it includes Note 45 on trade payables, with MSMED Act disclosures, principal amounts unpaid, interest paid, and trade payables ageing for 2025 and 2024. Note 46 presents earnings per share calculations, and Note 47 covers employee benefits: defined contribution plans (RPF, ESIC, etc.), defined benefit plans (gratuity, pension), and COVID-19 children education support.

It also includes other comprehensive income items that will not be reclassified to profit or loss, such as remeasurement of defined benefit plans and equity instruments, along with related income tax, for both years.

structure.title: Consolidated Statement of Cash Flow
key_items: A. Cash flow from operating activities
structure.summary: The text presents a consolidated statement of cash flows for the year ended March 31, 2025, with comparative figures for 2024, in millions. It details cash flows from operating activities, including profit before tax, adjustments for depreciation, impairments, finance costs, interest and dividend income, and fair value gains/losses, followed by working capital changes, cash generated from operations, and income tax paid, yielding net cash from operating activities. Investing activities cover purchase and disposal of property, plant and equipment, loans and inter-corporate deposits, investment purchases and sales, fixed deposits, subsidiary acquisition/disposal, interest and dividend received, resulting in net cash used in investing. Financing activities include borrowings and repayments, lease liability repayments, buy-back of non-controlling interests, working capital demand loans, finance costs, and dividends paid, yielding net cash used in financing. It reconciles net increase/decrease in cash, beginning and ending cash balances, and effects of exchange differences and subsidiary transitions.

structure.summary: This section presents Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Limited's consolidated statement of cash flow for the year ended March 31, 2025, including cash and cash equivalents, changes in financial liabilities/assets from financing activities with opening and closing balances, and a reference to lease liabilities, along with auditor's and board's signatures, company information, and material accounting policies. It covers the basis of consolidation, including control definition, non-controlling interests, intra-group eliminations, changes in ownership, and investments in associates and joint ventures using the equity method. It addresses current classification based on the operating cycle and business combinations using the acquisition method, including goodwill, contingent consideration, and non-controlling interest measurement. Foreign currency translation and segment reporting are detailed. Property, plant and equipment accounting covers cost, depreciation, useful lives, and review policies. Goodwill and other intangible assets, financial instruments, leases, inventories, provisions, revenue recognition, government grants, employee benefits, income taxes, exceptional items, recent pronouncements, and detailed disclosures are also included.

It also includes auditor's and board's signatures, company information, and material accounting policies covering fair value measurement, statement of compliance with Ind AS, basis of preparation (historical cost and accrual, with exceptions), and fair value hierarchy levels (1, 2, 3).

nodes.title: a. Basis of consolidation
nodes.summary: The text covers the basis of consolidation for consolidated financial statements, including the definition of control, power, and consolidation periods; attribution of profit or loss, other comprehensive income, and total comprehensive income to owners and non-controlling interests; line-by-line consolidation and elimination of intra-group balances, transactions, gains/losses, and cash flows; elimination of parent's investment and equity; uniform accounting policies. It also addresses changes in ownership interests without loss of control as equity transactions and recognition of gain/loss and reclassification of OCI upon loss of control. Finally, it covers investments in associates and joint ventures, including definitions of significant influence and joint control, application of the equity method, recognition of share of profits/losses and OCI, distribution adjustments, goodwill and impairment, discontinuation of the equity method, disposal calculations, and treatment of transactions with associates/joint ventures.

nodes.title: Consolidated Notes: Current Classification and Business Combinations
nodes.summary: The page covers two notes to consolidated financial statements. First, it defines the operating cycle (twelve months) for classifying assets and liabilities as current or non-current. Second, it details business combinations: criteria for identifying an acquired business (inputs and substantive processes), use of the acquisition method since April 1, 2015, determination of acquisition date and control, goodwill measurement, bargain purchase gains, consideration transferred (including contingent consideration), subsequent accounting for contingent consideration, acquisition-related costs, contingent liabilities, non-controlling interest measurement, treatment of step acquisitions, and provisional accounting adjustments.

nodes.title: Notes on Foreign Currency Accounting and Segment Reporting
nodes.summary: The page covers two notes to consolidated financial statements. Foreign currency section details translation of transactions and monetary items, recognition of exchange differences (with exceptions for construction assets, hedges, and foreign operations), treatment of non-monetary items, and translation of foreign operations including goodwill and fair value adjustments, with reclassification rules on disposal. Segment reporting section states operating segments are reported consistently with internal reporting to the chief operating decision maker, who allocates resources and assesses performance.

nodes.title: f. Property, plant and equipment
nodes.summary: This note covers accounting for property, plant and equipment (PPE): stated at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment, with freehold land not depreciated. Assets under construction are carried at cost including purchase price, eligible borrowing costs, and directly attributable costs; subsequent expenditures are capitalized only if they enhance future economic benefits. Depreciation starts when assets are ready for use, with separate accounting for major components having different useful lives. Depreciation is straight-line over useful lives (buildings 4-125 years, plant and equipment 2-30, vehicles 3-15, office equipment 2-17, furniture and fixtures 3-15), except freehold land and capital work-in-progress; leasehold improvements are depreciated over the shorter of lease term or useful life. Methods, useful lives, and residual values are reviewed annually with prospective effect. Software for internal use is capitalized as part of related PPE and amortized over the lower of its useful life or the remaining PPE useful life.

nodes.title: g. Goodwill and Other Intangible assets
nodes.summary: This section covers accounting policies for goodwill and other intangible assets, including impairment testing and amortization; research and development costs; de-recognition of intangible assets; financial instruments (debt and equity) with classification, measurement, de-recognition, and impairment under the expected credit loss model; financial liabilities and equity instruments, including compound instruments and hedge accounting; leases (lessee and lessor); inventories; provisions, contingencies, and restructuring; revenue recognition (goods, services, royalties, profit sharing, out-licensing, returns, contract assets/liabilities); government grants; employee benefits (defined benefit, defined contribution, termination, and other long-term benefits); income taxes (current, deferred, MAT, uncertain positions); exceptional items; recent accounting pronouncements; and detailed disclosures on property, plant, equipment, investments, and other financial statement items.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for Goodwill and Other Intangible assets. Goodwill is defined as excess consideration over fair value of identifiable net assets, measured at cost less impairment, allocated to cash-generating units, tested annually or when impairment indicators exist, with impairment losses recognized in profit and loss and not reversed, and included in disposal gain or loss calculations. Other Intangible assets with finite useful lives are measured at cost less accumulated amortization and impairment, with subsequent expenditures capitalized only when increasing future economic benefits.

nodes.title: Research and development
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for research and development (R&D) expenditure: research costs are expensed when incurred, while development costs are capitalized only if reliably measurable, technically and commercially feasible, with probable future economic benefits, and sufficient resources to complete. Capitalization typically begins after regulatory filing with high approval probability. Capitalized costs include materials and directly attributable expenses. Payments for in-licensed products are capitalized. Acquired in-process R&D is recognized as IPR&D, not amortized but tested annually for impairment. Milestone payments are recognized when the activity is performed. Subsequent expenditures are capitalized only if they enhance future economic benefits. Amortization is straight-line over 3-15 years for product and other intangibles, with useful lives and methods reviewed annually and changes applied prospectively.

nodes.title: De-recognition of intangible assets
nodes.summary: The text covers de-recognition of intangible assets, including gain/loss recognition; impairment of non-financial assets other than goodwill, detailing recoverable amount calculation, cash-generating units, loss allocation, and reversal conditions; non-current assets held for sale, covering classification criteria, measurement at lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, non-depreciation, and specific rules for subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures; and financial instruments, including initial recognition and measurement, and subsequent measurement categories for financial assets: amortised cost, FVTOCI, and FVTPL, with criteria and accounting treatment for each.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Financial Instruments and Debt Instruments
nodes.summary: The page outlines accounting policies from consolidated financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2025. It covers disposal of interests in associates/joint ventures and retained interest accounting under Ind AS 109, measurement of non-current assets held for sale at lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell without depreciation. It defines financial instruments and details financial assets' initial recognition at fair value plus transaction costs (except trade receivables), regular way trades, and subsequent measurement categories. It specifically explains debt instruments at amortised cost, including business model and SPPI criteria, effective interest rate method, and impairment recognition. It also covers debt instruments at FVTOCI, including qualifying criteria, fair value measurement, OCI recognition of fair value movements, recognition of interest income, impairment, foreign exchange in profit or loss, and reclassification on de-recognition.

nodes.title: Debt instrument at FVTPL
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies under Ind AS 109 for debt and equity instruments, de-recognition, and impairment of financial assets. Debt instruments are classified at FVTPL as a residual category or by election to eliminate accounting mismatch, measured at fair value through P&L. Equity instruments are measured at fair value; held-for-trading is FVTPL, while others may irrevocably elect FVTOCI with no recycling. De-recognition occurs when rights expire or transfer with risks/rewards or control, with continuing involvement recognized. Impairment uses the ECL model: simplified approach for trade receivables with lifetime ECL and provision matrix, and lifetime ECL for other financial assets if credit risk increases significantly.

nodes.title: Financial Instruments: Equity Instruments and De-recognition
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting for equity instruments and de-recognition of financial assets under Ind AS 109. Equity instruments are measured at fair value; held-for-trading instruments are classified as FVTPL, while others may irrevocably be elected as FVTOCI, with fair value changes (including foreign exchange, excluding dividends) recognized in OCI and no recycling. FVTPL equity instruments recognize all changes in profit or loss. De-recognition occurs when contractual cash flow rights expire or are transferred, or a pass-through arrangement exists with transfer of substantially all risks and rewards or control. If neither risks/rewards nor control are transferred, the asset is recognized to the extent of continuing involvement with an associated liability. On full de-recognition, the difference between carrying amount and consideration plus cumulative OCI gain/loss is recognized in profit or loss.

nodes.title: Impairment of financial assets
nodes.summary: The text covers impairment of financial assets under Ind AS 109, detailing the expected credit loss model, simplified approach for trade receivables, provision matrix, and treatment of other financial assets. It also addresses financial liabilities and equity instruments, including classification as debt or equity, equity instruments, compound financial instruments, initial recognition and measurement, subsequent measurement at amortised cost or FVTPL, and specific accounting for financial liabilities at FVTPL and amortised cost.

nodes.title: Financial Liabilities and Equity Instruments Accounting Policies
key_items: Financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for financial liabilities and equity instruments. It addresses classification as debt or equity based on contractual substance, recognition of equity instruments at proceeds net of costs, repurchase of own equity, and separate classification of compound instruments. Initial measurement of financial liabilities at fair value net of transaction costs is explained, including types like payables, borrowings, leases, guarantees, and derivatives. Subsequent measurement at amortized cost or FVTPL is described. For FVTPL liabilities, classification as held for trading or designated, treatment of gains/losses, and own credit risk effects in OCI or P&L are detailed. It also includes low credit risk simplification and write-off criteria for debt instruments at FVOCI.

nodes.title: Financial liabilities subsequently measured at amortised cost
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for financial liabilities at amortised cost, including EIR method and interest expense recognition. It details de-recognition criteria for liabilities replaced or modified. It discusses reclassification of financial assets, limited to debt instruments upon business model changes, applied prospectively. It describes derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting: initial and subsequent fair value measurement, gains/losses recognition, and hedge classification (fair value, cash flow, net investment). It outlines hedge documentation requirements and effectiveness assessment, and begins accounting for fair value hedges.

nodes.title: Financial Liabilities De-recognition and Financial Assets Reclassification
nodes.summary: The page covers two accounting topics. De-recognition: a financial liability is removed when discharged, cancelled, or expired; replacing or substantially modifying a liability with the same lender is treated as de-recognition of the original and recognition of a new liability, with the difference recognized in profit or loss. Reclassification of financial assets: classification is determined at initial recognition; equity instruments and financial liabilities are not reclassified, while debt instruments are reclassified only upon a change in business model, which is infrequent, determined by senior management due to significant external or internal changes, and applied prospectively from the reclassification date without restating prior gains, losses, or interest.

nodes.title: Derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting
nodes.summary: Covers derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting: initial recognition at fair value, subsequent remeasurement, and classification as assets or liabilities. Explains gains/losses treatment, including effective cash flow hedge portions in OCI. Describes hedge accounting categories: fair value hedges, cash flow hedges, and net investment hedges. Details formal designation and documentation requirements at hedge inception, including risk management objectives, hedge relationship, effectiveness assessment, and ongoing effectiveness evaluation. Provides accounting treatment for fair value hedges (immediate P&L recognition), cash flow hedges (effective portion in OCI, reclassification, and discontinuation rules), and net investment hedges (effective portion in FCTR, reclassification on disposal). Also mentions lease assessment at contract inception.

nodes.title: Group as a lessee
nodes.summary:
Group as a lessee
The Group applies the short-term lease recognition exemption to its short-term leases (i.e., those leases that have a lease term of 12 months or less from the commencement date and do not contain a purchase option). It also applies the lease of low-value assets recognition exemption to leases that are considered to be low value. Lease payments on short-term leases and leases of low-value assets are recognised as expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term.

nodes.title: Group as a lessor
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies: as a lessor, operating lease rental income is recognized on a straight-line basis, with inflation-linked increases recognized when accrued, initial direct costs added to the leased asset and recognized over the lease term, and contingent rents recognized as revenue when earned. Inventories (raw materials, packing materials, work-in-progress, stock-in-trade, stores and spares, finished goods) are measured at lower of cost (weighted average) and net realizable value, with cost components detailed; factors for slow-moving/obsolete inventory allowances are listed. Provisions, contingent liabilities, and contingent assets are addressed, including recognition criteria, reimbursements, discounting, restructuring provisions, onerous contracts, and disclosure of contingent liabilities/assets. Revenue from sale of goods is recognized when control transfers, with discussion of principal vs. agent, net revenue, variable consideration, and financing components.

nodes.title: Inventory, Provisions, Restructuring, Onerous Contracts, Contingencies, and Revenue Notes
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for inventory allowances (slow-moving, obsolete, non-saleable) based on shelf life, discontinuances, price changes, ageing, and competition. It details provisions, contingent liabilities and assets: recognition criteria, discounting, reimbursement, restructuring provisions (formal plan, direct costs), onerous contracts (unavoidable costs exceeding benefits), and contingent liabilities (possible obligations or present obligations with uncertain outflow) and assets (not recognised, disclosed if probable, recognised if virtually certain). Revenue from sale of goods is recognised on transfer of control, as principal, net of taxes, returns, chargebacks, rebates, and allowances, considering variable consideration, financing components, non-cash consideration, and consideration payable to customers.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition Policies in Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: This page outlines revenue recognition policies: profit sharing revenues (base price recognized on delivery, profit share when highly probable no reversal); out-licensing arrangements (upfront fees deferred over performance obligations, milestone payments recognized on achievement or over performance period); sales returns (accrual allowance based on historical experience and market factors); contract assets (conditional rights to consideration, subject to impairment); trade receivables (unconditional rights to consideration); contract liabilities (obligations for consideration received, recognized as revenue upon performance); and rendering of services (revenue recognized as services performed, upfront non-refundable payments deferred over service period).

nodes.title: Royalties
nodes.summary: The text covers accounting policies for royalties, dividends, interest, government grants, employee benefits (defined benefit plans, termination benefits, short-term and other long-term benefits, defined contribution plans), and income tax. Royalty revenue is recognized on an accrual basis per agreement substance when economic benefits are probable and measurable. Dividend income is recognized when the right to receive is established; interest income on a time basis using the effective interest rate. Government grants are recognized when reasonable assurance exists, with expense-related grants recognized over periods of related costs and asset-related grants deducted from asset carrying amount. Defined benefit gratuity plan uses projected unit credit method with actuarial valuations; actuarial gains/losses go to OCI. Termination benefits are recognized when demonstrably committed. Short-term leave is measured as additional amount expected to be paid; long-term leave is actuarially valued with gains/losses immediately in profit or loss. Defined contribution plans are expensed as services are received. Income tax expense includes current and deferred tax, recognized in profit or loss except items in OCI or equity.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Income, Government Grants, and Employee Benefits
key_items: Short-term and Other long-term employee benefits
nodes.summary: The page outlines accounting policies for dividend and interest income recognition, government grants, and employee benefits. Dividend income is recognized when the right to receive payment is established, and interest income is accrued using the effective interest method. Government grants are recognized when conditions are met and received, with expense-related grants recognized as income over the related cost periods and asset-related grants deducted from the asset's carrying amount. Employee benefits cover defined benefit plans (gratuity plan using projected unit credit method, with actuarial gains/losses in OCI), termination benefits (recognized when demonstrably committed or when voluntary redundancy offers are probable and estimable), and short-term and other long-term employee benefits (accumulated leave within 12 months as short-term, beyond 12 months as long-term using actuarial valuation, with gains/losses in profit or loss).
